Directory rule applies to descendants.

Frozen zlob gitignore suite: root rule does not match descendants.
Frozen zlob gitignore suite: slash-bearing rule is root-relative.
Frozen zlob gitignore suite: root-relative rule excludes only its exact prefix.
Frozen zlob gitignore suite: recursive directory rule.
Frozen zlob gitignore suite: recursive suffix below a literal root.
Frozen zlob gitignore suite: literal root prevents unrelated match.
Frozen zlob allowlist idiom, verified by Git: extensioned nested file is re-included.
Frozen zlob allowlist idiom: extensionless nested file stays ignored.
Frozen zlob gitignore suite: recursive middle segment.
A nested .gitignore re-includes what the root excluded: Git reads the file closest to the candidate last.
The nested negation names one file, so its siblings stay excluded by the root rule.
A nested file may add a rule the root never had.
A nested rule applies only below its own directory.
Three levels disagree; the deepest file wins, so the candidate is ignored again.
Git cannot re-include a file whose parent directory is excluded, so the negation has no effect.
Excluding the directory's contents rather than the directory itself leaves the negation effective.
Re-including a subtree needs both the directory and its contents named.
Git strips unescaped trailing whitespace from a rule.
A backslash-escaped trailing space is part of the rule and matches a name that ends in one.
A leading bang can be escaped, making the rule an ordinary exclusion of a file named with one.
A line starting with # is a comment, not a rule.
A blank line separates rules and matches nothing itself.
A leading **/ matches the directory at any depth.
A trailing /** matches everything below the directory.
A middle /**/ spans any number of directories.
A middle /**/ also spans zero directories, unlike the matcher's component-local reading.
Character classes are available in ignore rules.
A byte outside the class does not match.
Negated classes use the same ! spelling as the matcher.
POSIX class names work inside ignore rules.
A rule without a slash matches the basename at any depth.
A leading slash anchors the rule to the repository root.
A slash anywhere but at the end anchors the rule to the root.
The same rule therefore does not match the identical suffix deeper down.
A trailing slash restricts the rule to directories, and this candidate is a regular file.
The same rule ignores everything inside the directory it names.
A question mark matches one byte in an ignore rule too.
Wildcards in an ignore rule never match a separator, unlike the fnmatch-style matcher.
A star in an ignore rule stays inside one path component.
Repository excludes in .git/info/exclude apply like a root rule.
The root .gitignore outranks .git/info/exclude.
A nested .gitignore outranks .git/info/exclude as well.
A POSIX class name inside a bracket expression, matching.
The same class, not matching: the class is read, not taken literally.
Git does not expand braces in ignore rules.
The braces are literal, so the literal name matches.
An unanchored rule matches a whole component, not a suffix of one.
A double star in a rule spans whole components only.
Asterisks that are not a whole component are ordinary stars.
The same run, inside one component.
A trailing double star covers what is inside, not the directory itself.
An escaped trailing space is part of the name.
A rule ending in an unpaired backslash matches nothing.
A doubled separator creates an empty component, which Git treats as unmatchable.
Only one leading slash is an anchor; the second creates an unmatchable empty component.
Repeated interior separators create empty components and cannot hide a real path.
Git truncates an ignore rule at its first NUL byte.
The text after a NUL is not part of the ignore rule.
Git strips exactly one initial UTF-8 BOM, leaving a second BOM as part of the rule.
A slash inside a bracket class is not a path separator.
A slash after a POSIX class remains a bracket-class member.
A directory-only rule is evaluated against the directory entry itself, not only its descendants.
The explicit repository-local core.ignorecase setting folds a rule and candidate independently of the host filesystem.
A CRLF-terminated ignore line has the same rule text as its LF counterpart.
A class before a suffix star run ends Git's literal prefix, so the run is an ordinary star and cannot cross a separator.
A question mark before a suffix star run makes the run ordinary rather than directory-spanning.
An earlier star prevents a later suffix run from gaining special directory-spanning semantics.
A suffix run after an earlier wildcard is ordinary under Git's literal-prefix analysis.
An escaped star is literal and does not combine with the following star into a special run.
A special suffix star run may span directories, but its separator does not vanish to fuse two literal components.
The directory-spanning suffix run does not become an ordinary in-component star or erase its separator.
Even repeated special runs do not erase separators and fuse the surrounding literal components.
A final special star run retains its literal prefix, so an anchored negation re-includes the matching root entry after a catch-all rule.
Git's plain slash search anchors a rule even when the slash is inside a bracket class.
A slash beside a POSIX class anchors the rule to its ignore-file directory.
A class negating only slash accepts every candidate-component byte instead of becoming malformed when slash is removed.
A closing bracket in the first member position is literal; the following bracket closes the class.
A negated class can likewise use a closing bracket as its first literal member.
The literal first-member closing bracket remains excluded by the negated class.
A first-member closing bracket does not also close the class, so this spelling is unclosed and matches nothing.
A slash after a first-member closing bracket remains inside the class rather than splitting the rule.
The class-member slash still anchors the rule to its ignore-file directory.
Component splitting preserves the first-member closing bracket and slash in a negated class too.
A negated directory-only rule re-includes the directory entry itself after an earlier positive rule.
A symlink to a directory is still a symlink candidate, so a directory-only rule does not ignore the link itself.
Slash as a range's lower endpoint leaves the matchable 0-9 byte range intact.
Removing an unmatchable slash upper endpoint must not turn the adjacent dash into a literal class member.
A negated range with slash as its lower endpoint still excludes digits.
An escaped slash is semantically the same component separator as a plain slash.
An escaped separator after a special suffix star run retains the run's directory-spanning form.
The special suffix run before an escaped separator may also match zero bytes.
